title: Evaluating Context Compaction on the Questions That Come Later

paper.title: Evaluating Context Compaction on the Questions That Come Later
paper.abstract:
Abstract Language-model agents compact their context for the question at hand, but the compacted context must also serve
questions that come later. We evaluate compaction on these later questions, using four corpora that annotate the
evidence of several questions per text and recorded agent trajectories, and compare every method with random
deletion at the same budget. On MultiRC, keeping the sentences that gpt-6-luna (through the OpenAI Decisions API) judges
necessary for the current question raises its accuracy on that question by 11.4 points at 25% of the tokens. On the later questions,
however, no method that selects sentences for the current question does detectably better than deleting sentences at
random. Deleting words instead of sentences does better: LLMLingua-2 , which ignores the question, beats random sentence
deletion at the same token count by 12.5 points on the later MultiRC
questions. It keeps about twice random deletion’s share of the evidence’s content words, and at equal content-word
retention its gain shrinks to 7.3 points (exploratory). On
FEVER, label accuracy can overstate what the kept text supports: the gain of sentence selection is no longer detected
when answers are scored against the kept evidence, and the 21.0-point gain of LLMLingua-2 is not shown to rest on the kept text. The ranking also
depends on the setting: on Evidence Inference sentence selection beats LLMLingua-2 at a nominal 25% budget, and on τ \tau -bench trajectories, whose later tool calls need exact identifiers, it beats random deletion while LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain. Scores on the question a compaction was made for do not reliably show how it serves later
ones.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Applications that call a language model many times, such as agents, assistants and multi-step pipelines, carry text from one call to the next: documents read so far, conversation turns, tool outputs. We call this text the state . Every call pays for it in tokens and the context window bounds it, so applications compact it: they delete parts of it to fit a budget. At compaction time the application usually knows its current question, and the natural choice is to keep what that question needs. The state, however, outlives that question. Later questions, unknown when the deletion was made, must be answered from whatever survived, and a deleted sentence is gone for all of them. We call the question available at compaction time known and the later ones hidden . Query-aware compressors are usually evaluated on the question they compress for; we evaluate them on the hidden ones. The columns give the probabilities the same model assigns after reading each text: that the gold answer is correct, and that the text contains what the hidden question needs (the sufficiency check of Section 3 ). We compare query-aware selection, which keeps what the known question needs, with question-agnostic compressors. Our main instance uses typed decision models , which take a state and typed questions about it (a Boolean, a Choice among options or a Score) and return a probability for each answer ( TypeSafe AI, 2026 ; OpenAI, 2026 ) . Typed selection asks one Boolean per sentence, “is this sentence needed to answer the question?”, and keeps the most probable sentences; the same model then answers the questions, and in this role we call it the reader . Figure 1 shows the risk. We compare it with random deletion, question-agnostic selection by the same model, TF-IDF (term frequency–inverse document frequency) selection and lead (the first sentences). We also run LLMLingua-2 ( Pan et al., 2024 ) , which deletes individual words without any question, and, at token budgets, LongLLMLingua ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) and maximal marginal relevance (MMR; Carbonell & Goldstein, 1998 ), two established compressors that use the question. The corpora are MultiRC ( Khashabi et al., 2018 ; Wang et al., 2019 ) , ERASER’s FEVER ( Thorne et al., 2018 ; DeYoung et al., 2020 ) , Evidence Inference ( Lehman et al., 2019 ) and LoCoMo conversation memory ( Maharana et al., 2024 ) , in which several questions share one text and each question’s evidence is annotated, and recorded τ \tau -bench agent trajectories ( Yao et al., 2024 ) , whose questions ask for the identifiers that later tool calls pass. Our findings are: • Selection for the known question beats random deletion on that question. On MultiRC, typed selection, MMR and LongLLMLingua raise known-question accuracy over random deletion at 25%, but none shows a detected advantage on hidden questions on average. On MultiRC, hidden questions gain only where they share the known question’s evidence. On FEVER, a gain in recovering a claim’s label is not detected when the kept text is scored for what it supports (Section 3 ). The label-accuracy gain of word-level compression there is not shown to rest on the kept text either (Section 4 ). • On MultiRC, picking words beats picking sentences by the same scores. With the same importance scores, picking words instead of sentences raises hidden-question accuracy, and LLMLingua-2 and a hybrid of typed sentences and LLMLingua-2 words lead on hidden questions. They keep about as many evidence words as random deletion but far more of the evidence’s content words, which partly explains the lead: at equal content-word retention it shrinks from 12.5 to 7.3 points with gpt-6-luna (Section 4 ). • The ordering is not stable across settings. On Evidence Inference typed selection beats LLMLingua-2 on hidden claims at a nominal 25% budget. On agent trajectories, whose later calls need exact identifiers, typed selection beats random deletion and LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain (Section 5 ). Concurrent work shows that compaction can serve the current query and fail later ones ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Zhang, 2026 ) . We add an evaluation on annotated evidence that compares sentence- and word-level compression and locates where each serves later questions.

sections.heading: 2 Evaluation setup
sections.text: This section describes the MultiRC experiment; Sections 3 and 5 give the changes for the other settings.

sections.heading: Data and models.
sections.text: Each MultiRC question has several candidate answers that annotators labeled correct or incorrect, and a question can have more than one correct answer. We use 300 paragraphs with at least three questions and 6–20 sentences, with 3,355 questions and 17,895 candidate answers, from the validation and training splits (validation alone has too few such paragraphs). The first listed question of each paragraph is known and the others are hidden. gpt-6-luna reads every corpus. Every gpt-6-luna read and selection in this paper goes through the OpenAI Decisions API ( OpenAI, 2026 ) , the typed decision interface: a request poses typed questions and returns a probability for each answer, with no generated text. Three open-weight models built for the typed decision interface, open-decider (2B), open-bosun (1.7B) and open-lumma (0.6B) ( Mapika, 2026 ; Hanno Labs, 2026 ; FrontiersMind, 2026 ) , also read MultiRC from their released weights, and qwen3.8-flash is a general instruction-tuned reader (Appendix B ). We drop refused answers; counting them as wrong instead changes neither the sign of any typed − - random contrast nor whether its interval excludes zero (Appendix B ).

sections.heading: Selectors and budgets.
sections.text: Both model-based selectors ask one Boolean per sentence, with the sentences numbered in the state. Typed selection puts the known question in the state and asks “is sentence i i needed to answer the question?”. Question-agnostic selection gives no question and asks “does sentence i i state a fact that a reader is likely to be asked about later?”. A policy keeps a budget b ∈ { 25 , 50 , 75 } % b\in\{25,50,75\}\% of a paragraph’s sentences (rounded half to even, at least one). Typed and agnostic selection keep the most probable sentences, TF-IDF selection those closest to the known question, lead the first ones, and random deletion one seeded uniform sample. Kept sentences stay in document order. Token-matched tests cut every text, LLMLingua-2 ’s included, to the same o200k token count (Appendix G ).

sections.heading: Reading and measures.
sections.text: One request asks one Boolean per candidate answer: “given the passage, is this a correct answer to the question?”, where “no” is defined as “not supported or incorrect”. Once a compaction deletes the evidence for a correct answer, the reader is therefore asked to reject that answer. We score each candidate answer against the MultiRC labels, average within each paragraph, then over paragraphs, with paragraph-bootstrap 95% intervals; a difference is detected when its interval excludes zero. Answering “no” to every candidate already scores 55.6%, and of the four typed readers only gpt-6-luna (88.2%) and open-decider (75.3%) are detectably above it on the full text, so the main tables report these two. A hidden question is overlapping if its annotated evidence shares a sentence with the known question’s, and disjoint otherwise.

sections.heading: Prespecified analyses.
sections.text: Hypotheses, tests and decision rules were specified before any model request for the Evidence Inference overlap test, the KEEP–DROP contrast, the LoCoMo test and four follow-ups under one plan (token-matched budgets, query-aware baselines, three-way labels and harder LoCoMo options). The same holds for the LLMLingua-2 granularity test, the hybrid compactor, a test with a different known question, a general-reader test, the τ \tau -bench test and the abstractive-summary test. Appendix A counts the outcomes and lists every prediction that was not fully met. The other analyses, including the content-word analysis and the FEVER evidence-support check of Section 4 , are exploratory. The ancillary files contain the summary tables and the values of all reported numbers.

sections.heading: The known question gains.
sections.text: At a 25% budget, open-decider answers the known question at 70% after typed selection, against 61% after random deletion and 74% on the full text; for gpt-6-luna the same accuracies are 77%, 67% and 89% (compacted texts in Table 1 ).

sections.heading: Averaged over hidden questions, selection stays near random deletion.
sections.text: Typed − - random hidden accuracy is slightly below zero for both readers at 25% and 50%, and question-agnostic selection is similarly close to random (Table 1 ). The split holds when texts are cut to the same token count: typed − - random at 25% with gpt-6-luna is +11.4 [ +9.1 , +13.8 ] points on the known question and − - 0.4 [ − - 1.5 , +0.6 ] on hidden ones. LongLLMLingua and MMR show the same split with both readers, and on hidden questions LongLLMLingua falls below random deletion ( − - 1.6 [ − - 2.6 , − - 0.6 ] with gpt-6-luna ; Appendix G ). With qwen3.8-flash as reader, typed − - random is +10.4 [ +7.4 , +13.3 ] on the known question and − - 0.6 [ − - 1.8 , +0.6 ] on hidden ones. sections.heading: Hidden questions gain where they share the known question’s evidence.
sections.text: ERASER ( DeYoung et al., 2020 ) marks evidence sentences for 3,300 of the 3,355 MultiRC questions. Typed selection at 25% keeps 50% of the known question’s evidence ( gpt-6-luna ) against 25% expected for a random subset, and about the random share for hidden questions. Hidden questions that share evidence with the known one gain +4.3 [ +2.2 , +6.4 ] points ( gpt-6-luna ) and +5.3 [ +2.9 , +7.7 ] ( open-decider ). Disjoint ones lose − - 2.9 [ − - 4.3 , − - 1.4 ] and − - 3.0 [ − - 4.5 , − - 1.4 ], with less of their evidence kept than under random deletion (18% against 25%; Figure 2 ).

sections.heading: Deleted evidence drives the losses.
sections.text: A hidden answer that was right on the full text flips more often when its evidence was deleted. With gpt-6-luna , adding some of the deleted evidence back undoes more flips than adding as many sentences that are evidence for no question ( +26.8 [ +22.6 , +31.5 ] points; Appendix D ). A sufficiency check (“does the passage contain the information needed to answer this question?”) ranks questions with broken evidence first. Yet re-reading a random quarter of hidden questions on the full text recovers most of what re-reading the lowest-sufficiency quarter does (Appendix D ).

sections.heading: FEVER and Evidence Inference: hidden claims gain in label recovery.
sections.text: Each question here is a claim, and the reader judges whether the text supports it. We sample 200 FEVER documents with 5,433 hidden claims and 792 Evidence Inference clinical-trial articles (Appendix E ); the first claim of each document is known. On FEVER at 25% typed − - random hidden-claim accuracy is +17.2 points, and on Evidence Inference disjoint claims gain too, with more of their evidence kept than random deletion keeps (Figure 2 ).

sections.heading: Label recovery and support scoring disagree.
sections.text: Label accuracy counts the document’s label as right even when a claim’s evidence was deleted. A prespecified three-way read therefore also scores each answer against what the kept text supports: the document’s label if all of the claim’s annotated evidence was kept and “not enough info” if all of it was deleted. In this read, with true and false claims weighted equally, typed selection on FEVER recovers the label 25.2 points more often than random deletion, while its support-target accuracy, with the three targets weighted equally, differs from random deletion by − - 1.0 [ − - 3.9 , +2.2 ] points (Appendix J ). Prespecified KEEP–DROP tests give a hidden claim two texts with the same number of sentences, one with its evidence and one without; KEEP beats DROP by +50.0 [ +47.4 , +52.4 ] points on FEVER and +17.8 [ +15.9 , +19.7 ] on Evidence Inference (Appendix K ).

sections.heading: For sentence selection, the gain follows the extra evidence kept.
sections.text: Across the eight 25% groups of Figure 2 (corpus, reader, overlapping or disjoint), the typed − - random hidden gain rises with how much more of the hidden questions’ evidence typed selection keeps than random deletion, at 0.37 0.37 points of gain per point of extra evidence. We fixed this line before a second experiment that repeats typed selection with a different, randomly drawn known question in every document. On the eight new groups it misses the observed gains by 3.4 points on average. The largest misses are 9.5 points (overlapping FEVER claims, under-predicted) and 6.9 (overlapping MultiRC questions read by open-decider , over-predicted); the other six are within 4.8 points (Appendix F ).

sections.heading: Word-level compression leads on hidden questions.
sections.text: LLMLingua-2 − - random sentence deletion on hidden questions with annotated evidence, from the model of Appendix I without retention terms, is +12.5 [ +11.3 , +13.6 ] points on MultiRC with gpt-6-luna , +6.0 [ +4.7 , +7.3 ] with open-decider and +21.0 [ +18.7 , +23.4 ] in label accuracy on FEVER; the paired contrast over all hidden questions, dropping refusals pairwise, gives +12.1 and +21.0 for the two gpt-6-luna cells (Appendix G ). LLMLingua-2 is also ahead of typed selection on hidden questions in all three cells (Table 2 ). The hybrid beats typed selection on hidden questions in all three cells, by 4.6 to 8.3 points with every interval above zero; it beats LLMLingua-2 on FEVER and stays below it on MultiRC (Appendix H ).

sections.heading: The gain comes from picking words.
sections.text: A prespecified test keeps the LLMLingua-2 scores and changes only the unit kept. Picking words instead of whole sentences raises hidden-question accuracy at 25% by +11.7 points (MultiRC, gpt-6-luna ), +4.6 (MultiRC, open-decider ) and +19.1 (FEVER). Whole sentences picked by the same scores are not detectably better than random sentence deletion in five of six cells (Appendix H ). On the known MultiRC question LLMLingua-2 is ahead of typed selection with gpt-6-luna in all four comparisons. The two intervals at sentence budgets exclude zero, and the one at 50% of the tokens just does (upper end − 0.02 -0.02 points) (Appendices G and H ).

sections.heading: Word-level compression keeps the evidence’s content words.
sections.text: Counted over all words, LLMLingua-2 , the hybrid and random sentence deletion keep similar shares of the hidden questions’ evidence on MultiRC, yet their accuracies differ by up to 12.5 points. Sentence deletion keeps a sentence’s content and function words together. LLMLingua-2 drops function words first, so it keeps 48.0% of the evidence’s content words against 26.1% for random sentence deletion (Table 2 ). For sentence policies the two counts agree within half a point, so the relation of Section 3 is unchanged.

sections.heading: Content-word retention accounts for part of the lead.
sections.text: A model of each answer’s correctness, with document fixed effects, compares policies at equal content-word retention. It describes an association, since the policies produce the retention they are compared at. At equal retention the MultiRC LLMLingua-2 − - random-sentence gap shrinks from 12.5 to +7.3 [ +6.1 , +8.4 ] points with gpt-6-luna and from 6.0 to +2.0 [ +0.7 , +3.2 ] with open-decider . Also conditioning on how many of each candidate answer’s content words survive leaves +4.9 points with gpt-6-luna and +0.6 [ − - 0.5 , +1.8 ] with open-decider . The hybrid − - typed gaps shrink the same way (Table 15 ). On FEVER binned retention leaves 1.3 points; a linear term leaves 14.9, because accuracy rises non-linearly with retention there.

sections.heading: Which words are kept matters too.
sections.text: On FEVER typed selection keeps more of the hidden claims’ content words than LLMLingua-2 yet scores lower (Table 2 ). At the same content-word retention LLMLingua-2 still beats random word deletion by +6.7 [ +5.5 , +8.0 ] points on MultiRC with gpt-6-luna , +1.7 [ +0.5 , +2.9 ] with open-decider and +9.6 [ +7.5 , +11.7 ] on FEVER (Appendix I ).

sections.heading: LLM-written summaries stay below word-level compression.
sections.text: A compaction can also have an LLM rewrite the text. Two summarizers, qwen3.8-flash and gpt-6.1-sol , summarized each MultiRC paragraph within the same token budget, once for unknown later questions and once for the known question (Appendix O ). On hidden questions the generic summaries beat random sentence deletion by 7.6 and 10.9 points but stay below LLMLingua-2 : summary − - LLMLingua-2 is − - 4.5 [ − - 5.7 , − - 3.2 ] and − - 1.3 [ − - 2.4 , − - 0.3 ] points. The summaries written for the known question answer it better than typed selection and LLMLingua-2 (88.5% and 89.2%), but on hidden questions they fall below random deletion ( qwen3.8-flash , − - 2.9 [ − - 4.0 , − - 1.8 ]) or show no detected gain ( gpt-6.1-sol , +0.9 [ − - 0.2 , +2.1 ]).

sections.heading: On FEVER, label accuracy overstates the word-level gain.
sections.text: FEVER accuracy counts the document’s label, which Section 3 shows can be right without textual support. The LLMLingua-2 gain over random sentence deletion lies on true claims ( +31.5 [ +28.0 , +35.0 ] points; false claims − - 2.2 [ − - 3.7 , − - 1.0 ]). When at most a fifth of a true claim’s evidence content words survive, the reader still calls it supported for 56.0% of claims after LLMLingua-2 and 26.8% after random sentence deletion. An evidence-support target, scored on the binary reads, reproduces the three-way result for typed − - random ( − - 0.2 [ − - 3.4 , +3.0 ] points, label-balanced) and removes the hybrid’s gain over typed selection ( − - 3.7 [ − - 9.4 , +1.3 ]). Under LLMLingua-2 it is undefined for 99% of hidden claims, whose evidence is partly kept, so its FEVER gain is not shown to rest on the kept text (Appendix I ).

sections.heading: Evidence Inference.
sections.text: On Evidence Inference typed selection keeps more of even the disjoint claims’ evidence than random deletion (Figure 2 ). It beats LLMLingua-2 on hidden claims when LLMLingua-2 is set to the compression rate of 25% sentence deletion ( +12.2 [ +10.1 , +14.4 ] points); at the 50% rate the difference is +1.0 [ − - 0.5 , +2.6 ]. This comparison is not token-matched: at 25% the typed texts keep 28.9% of the article’s o200k tokens and the LLMLingua-2 texts 25.8% (Appendices G and L ).

sections.heading: Agent trajectories.
sections.text: In the recorded τ \tau -bench retail trajectories an agent calls tools for a simulated user. The state is a trajectory up to its middle tool output, split into turns, tool calls and tool outputs. The known question asks which identifier (an order, item, product or payment-method ID, or a zip code) the next tool call passes; each hidden question asks the same for a later call, among same-shaped identifiers from the state. On 390 states with 837 hidden questions at 25% of the tokens, typed − - random is +22.3 [ +15.1 , +28.9 ] points with gpt-6-luna and +21.7 [ +15.7 , +27.6 ] with qwen3.8-flash , while LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain ( +4.0 [ − - 1.1 , +9.3 ]); token-level extractive compressors are known to strip the action syntax that agents need ( Zhang & Sun, 2026 ) . Typed selection keeps the hidden question’s identifier for 66.4% of hidden questions against 42.4% (random) and 52.3% ( LLMLingua-2 ).

sections.heading: Anticipating later calls costs the known one.
sections.text: Selectors that anticipate later calls trade the known call for the hidden ones: on a 120-state subsample, expected-coverage selection gains +12.8 [ +5.2 , +20.8 ] points over typed selection on hidden questions and − - 10.6 (90% interval [ − - 17.8, − - 2.9]) on the known one. About half of the hidden gain comes from fewer refusals: scored on answered questions only, it is +5.8 [ − - 1.4 , +13.6 ] (Appendix N ).

sections.heading: Conversation memory.
sections.text: LoCoMo’s ten long conversations are compacted four times as they grow, so a dropped turn never returns. At the last checkpoint, a typed 25% memory with a hidden question’s evidence beats one with the same number of turns without it by 13.3 points ( gpt-6-luna ), in all 10 conversations. Typed versus random deletion is unresolved for both readers, and on the four-choice format empty memory already scores 81.4% (Appendix M ).

sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: Query-aware sentence selection raises the known question’s accuracy over random deletion. On later questions it helps those that share the known question’s evidence. On MultiRC, where many do not, it does no better than random deletion on average. On MultiRC the compressors that lead on later questions delete words. They drop function words first, so the same token budget holds more of the evidence’s content words. At equal content-word retention two fifths to two thirds of LLMLingua-2 ’s MultiRC lead over random sentence deletion disappears, and LLMLingua-2 still beats random words, so which words are kept also matters. On FEVER, typed selection’s label gain is not detected under support scoring, and the word-level gain is not shown to rest on the kept text. The ordering is not general. On Evidence Inference, where even disjoint claims keep more evidence under typed selection, it beats LLMLingua-2 at a nominal 25% budget. On agent trajectories, whose later calls need exact identifiers, LLMLingua-2 keeps fewer of them than typed selection and shows no detected gain. For evaluation, the results suggest scoring hidden questions as well as the known one, comparing with random deletion at matched tokens, measuring the hidden questions’ evidence kept in content words, and reporting support-based scoring next to label recovery. Compaction also costs tokens to build: for typed selection at 25% with gpt-6-luna , compacting once pays for itself in input tokens only with one request per later question, after about 6.6 to 11.0 of them on FEVER, Evidence Inference and LoCoMo. On Evidence Inference this is more than its mean of 3.7 later questions, and on MultiRC the extrapolated break-even, 14.0, exceeds its mean of 10.2 (Appendix L ). Keeping the full state allows a re-read for a later question, but neither recovery we tested matches it. On MultiRC, re-reading the lowest-sufficiency quarter of hidden questions on the full text lifts accuracy over all hidden questions from 67% to 74%, against 89% on the full text (Appendix D ). On agent trajectories, fetching dropped units on demand reaches 69.1% against 88.8% for the full state at 102.0% of its passage tokens, and the prespecified prediction that it would come close is not met (Appendix N ).

sections.heading: 7 Related work
sections.text: Prompt compression removes tokens or sentences by perplexity ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) , by query-aware importance ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) or by a learned task-agnostic importance ( Pan et al., 2024 ) , and key–value (KV) cache compression has the same split ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . Earlier agent-memory work studied the same write-before-query asymmetry. TierMem ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) falls back to a raw log when a router judges pre-query summaries insufficient, and EMBER ( Li et al., 2026 ) learns which evidence to retain before the query. Chen et al. (2026) find that query-aware KV eviction does not generalize across queries, and Yu et al. (2026) separate write-time from retrieval-time loss. We delete sentences (turns on LoCoMo) for one known question and test the questions hidden at deletion time with annotated evidence and KEEP–DROP substitutions. The closest work is concurrent. Tirmazi et al. (2026) formalize compaction against later queries, with a set-membership case study, and Liu et al. (2026) find that compacting agent KV caches before later queries arrive hurts, and that deferring compaction recovers much of the cost; RestoreKV ( Baek et al., 2026 ) adds learned restoration to query-agnostic eviction, and Luo et al. (2026) find that hiding the question at compression time reorders KV-cache compressors, with most no better than trivial baselines. These work on KV caches rather than on evidence-annotated text. Liu (2026) counts the extra retrieval calls an agent makes to re-acquire state that compression dropped, and Zhang (2026) tests whether compressed memory keeps what a later update needs on synthetic histories; we measure answer accuracy on later questions of existing corpora and locate the loss with evidence annotations. Wang et al. (2026) find that context compactors keep about a sixth of the constraints a user sets for the agent’s later behavior. Sadowski & Chudziak (2026) and Shen & Li (2026) optimize what is written when the later goal is known. Mnemon ( Wang, 2026 ) uses the same per-record “is this needed” Boolean but keeps its raw records recoverable. Shankaranarayana et al. (2026) find that asking whether the evidence suffices is more informative than answer confidence; we ask it after compaction has deleted part of the evidence. Ai et al. (2026) find that KV-cache eviction can keep final-answer accuracy while the reasoning that supports the answer degrades; on FEVER we find the analogous gap between label accuracy and the evidence the kept text retains.

sections.heading: 8 Limitations
sections.text: The experiments use public text and conversation benchmarks and recorded agent trajectories, not live agents. Abstractive summaries are tested only on MultiRC at a 25% budget. In the τ \tau -bench test the actions and tool outputs are fixed by the recording, the questions ask only for identifiers, retail is the only domain with enough trajectories for inference, and the only budget is 25%. The relation between gain and evidence kept is tested by consistency across settings, KEEP–DROP interventions and one out-of-sample check on the three document corpora, for sentence selection; it could not be assessed on LoCoMo and holds only qualitatively on τ \tau -bench. The content-word analysis of word-level compression is exploratory, leaves part of the MultiRC gap unexplained and, on FEVER, does not separate content words from all words. The model-based sentence selectors are typed models, which usually also answer; qwen3.8-flash is the only general instruction-tuned reader, and it reads the texts that gpt-6-luna selected. Only two typed readers perform above the all-“no” baseline on MultiRC. On the three document corpora the known question is the first listed one or, in one test, one other randomly drawn question per document. Evidence annotations are incomplete, so neither the retention tests nor the evidence-support target can account for unannotated evidence. Budgets count sentences or conversation turns, except in the token-matched tests and the τ \tau -bench test; Appendix L counts input tokens. The KEEP–DROP comparison covers one budget and does not include MultiRC. LoCoMo has ten conversations and a four-choice format on which empty memory already scores 81.4%. Hosted reads taken at different times can differ slightly (Appendix C ). Intervals are unadjusted for multiple comparisons. The benchmark texts predate the models, so contamination cannot be ruled out.

sections.heading: Broader Impact Statement
sections.text: Compaction that deletes a question’s evidence can make supported answers “unsupported”. Without provenance, a downstream consumer may take them for answers that are genuinely unsupported or false, and the sufficiency check does not flag every such case. Recoverable full-state designs should be evaluated before compaction is used in consequential settings. Keeping the full state in turn carries the privacy and retention obligations of whatever it contains. The Evidence Inference articles are clinical-trial reports used only as a benchmark, and compaction and the sufficiency check remain unvalidated for clinical decision support.

sections.heading: Texts.
sections.text: The analyses use, for each MultiRC paragraph, the original text and fifteen compactions (the five sentence policies of Section 2 at three budgets), plus the additional random masks of Appendix C . LLMLingua-2 texts, at 25% and 50%, are read separately (Appendix G ).

sections.heading: Coverage and request size.
sections.text: open-decider ’s 75% rows cover 166–171 paragraphs and its other rows, like gpt-6-luna ’s, cover 300; open-bosun reads the first 100 paragraphs. The open-weight models are released as decider-2b, bosun-v3.1-1.7b and Lumma-fev-0.6b. The Decisions API accepts at most 200 questions per request, so the 38 read requests above that limit are split into chunks of 125 questions.

sections.heading: Repeat reads.
sections.text: open-decider reads deterministically up to floating point. Each read is one forward pass in evaluation mode with a softmax over option logits, no sampling and a fixed option order. Each question has its own row, unaffected by the others in the request. Repeated runs of hosted language models can differ ( Ouyang et al., 2025 ; Atıl et al., 2025 ) . For gpt-6-luna , across 100 repeated full-text reads, all 6,603 answers were identical. Its sufficiency checks take few distinct values, which is why ties at the cut are re-read in proportion.

sections.heading: Averages.
sections.text: Paragraph-macro averages weigh each paragraph equally, with answers averaged within it; bootstrap intervals use 2000 resamples (macro-averaged accuracies and contrasts). The pooled flip-rate risk differences of Section 3 use 1000. The intervals of the sufficiency AUROC against flipped answers and of the re-read gain over a random quarter (MultiRC and FEVER) use 500.

sections.heading: Selection details.
sections.text: A budget b b keeps max ⁡ ( 1 , round ⁡ ( b ​ n ) ) \max(1,\mathrm{round}(bn)) of a paragraph’s n n sentences. The score-based policies keep the highest-scoring sentences, ties going to the earlier sentence. TF-IDF selection fits scikit-learn’s TfidfVectorizer (English stop words, other settings default) on the paragraph’s sentences plus the known question and ranks sentences by cosine similarity to the question.

sections.heading: Refusals.
sections.text: In the sentence-budget MultiRC reads, 710 of gpt-6-luna ’s answers came back as refusals rather than probabilities; they came from 290 requests and were all candidate-answer Booleans. We drop each refused answer from every statistic that needs it. Refusals are rare: under the five sentence policies at 25% and 50%, at most 1.2% of a policy’s known or hidden answers are refused (Table 4 a). At token-matched budgets the highest share in the follow-ups is LongLLMLingua’s, 4.8% of hidden answers at 25%; in the granularity test random word deletion draws 6.4% at 25%, so its contrasts rest on the answers it receives. The open-weight readers never refuse.

sections.text: The plan fixed the reader, texts and estimators and two predictions. qwen3.8-flash ’s full-text MultiRC accuracy is above the all-“no” rate, with the interval above it (R1), and typed − - random on the known question at 25% is positive on each corpus (R2); hidden contrasts and the overlap split are reported without predictions.

sections.heading: Reader: design.
sections.text: qwen3.8-flash answers one yes/no question per call, with the paper’s read instructions; the probability of “yes” is taken from the first-token log-probabilities of “yes” and “no” (thinking off) and thresholded at 0.5. It reads the paper’s texts: the full text and typed selection ( gpt-6-luna ’s selection), question-agnostic selection (MultiRC and FEVER; Evidence Inference has no question-agnostic texts) and random deletion (the paper’s mask) at 25% and 50% of the sentences, and on MultiRC and FEVER the token-matched LLMLingua-2 text at 25%. In all, 337,455 calls; the provider’s content filter refused the answers on 18 MultiRC paragraphs and one FEVER document (0.9–2.8% of MultiRC answers per text), which are dropped as refusals. gpt-6-luna reads the empty text with the paper’s read requests. Estimators are the paper’s.

sections.heading: Appendix C Random deletion over several masks
sections.text: The main text compares each policy with one seeded random mask per paragraph and budget. Here every contrast with random is recomputed against the mean over several seeded masks: 6 per paragraph for gpt-6-luna on MultiRC and FEVER, 11 for open-decider and 4–7 on Evidence Inference, the main mask included. A document’s contrast is the mean over its masks of the paired policy − - random difference, and the bootstrap resamples documents (2000 resamples) and keeps each document’s mask average. Table 6 gives the hidden-question contrasts. On MultiRC the 90% intervals of all 12 hidden-question contrasts with random (the eight of Table 6 and four from open-decider ’s re-read) have a largest absolute end of 1.6 points, and typed selection still beats random on the known question ( gpt-6-luna +9.7 [+7.2, +11.9] and open-decider +8.6 [+6.0, +11.4] points at 25%). Across single masks, gpt-6-luna ’s typed − - random on hidden MultiRC questions at 25% ranges from − - 0.8 to +0.3 points, and the main-text mask gives the lowest value. Two cells differ from the one-mask results: the MultiRC disjoint contrast excludes zero in all four reader-budget cells, and the FEVER disjoint contrast at 50% is below random. FEVER agnostic − - random still spans zero at both budgets, and on Evidence Inference H1 remains supported and H2 contradicted. sections.heading: Answers flip more often when evidence was deleted.
sections.text: Of the hidden answers the reader got right on the full text, under typed selection at 25% open-decider flips 14% when their evidence is intact and 36% when it is broken, a difference of +22 [+19, +25] points; for gpt-6-luna the rates are 5% and 29% (+24 [+21, +26]). gpt-6-luna reads all texts of this experiment. The restore and placebo texts keep the compacted sentences and add the chosen ones, in document order. Each is read with the paragraph’s original question set, split into requests of at most 125 questions as in that read, so only the state differs from the typed-selection 25% read. Recovery rates and accuracies are pooled over candidate answers of broken-evidence hidden questions, not paragraph-macro averages; intervals are paragraph bootstraps (2000 resamples) of the restore − - placebo recovery difference.

sections.heading: Design and results.
sections.text: On each eligible paragraph let m m be the number of deleted sentences that are evidence for no question and U U the deleted evidence of the broken hidden questions; the dose is d = min ⁡ ( m , | U | ) d=\min(m,|U|) , and paragraphs with m = 0 m=0 are skipped (61 of 297). Restore adds d d sentences drawn from U U (seeded per paragraph) and the placebo d d non-evidence sentences, so in 166 paragraphs restore adds only part of the deleted evidence. Restore and placebo reads are interleaved in time. Over 11,296 answers (the 166 answers refused in any of the full, compacted, restore and placebo reads are excluded), accuracy goes from 68% compacted to 78% with restore and 71% with the placebo (full text 89%). Of the 2,795 broken-evidence flips, restore undoes 46% and the placebo 20% (+27 [+23, +32]). On the 801 flips whose question got all its deleted evidence back, the rates are 86% and 21% (+65 [+59, +71]), and on the other 1,994, 31% and 19%. Adding all of the deleted evidence (7.4 sentences on average) against a placebo of as many non-evidence sentences where available (2.6 on average) gives +81 [+78, +84] points over 297 paragraphs.

sections.heading: FEVER.
sections.text: At 25% typed selection’s known-claim accuracy is 92% (full text 92%, random 56%). Agnostic − - random on the hidden claims is +2.1 [ − - 1.7, +5.8] points at 25% and +3.5 [ − - 0.2, +7.1] at 50%. At 25%, hidden claims judged correctly on the full text flip at 45% when their evidence was broken and 1% when it survived. Unlike on MultiRC, the sufficiency check ranks flipped claims better (AUROC 0.87 [0.85, 0.88]) than deleted evidence (0.77), and re-reading its lowest quarter lifts question-level accuracy from 71% to 86% (random 77%), a gain of +8.9 [+8.3, +9.4] points over a random quarter. Each read asks, per claim, “given the passage, is this claim supported?” and the sufficiency check. The 200 documents (14.7 sentences and 28.2 claims on average, one sentence per line) are a seeded sample of the ERASER FEVER documents with 8–40 sentences and no empty line that carry at least 3 distinct claims. All but 4 claims have a single label (SUPPORTS or REFUTES) and sentence-level evidence lying entirely in that document (71% of claims are SUPPORTS). A claim’s evidence is the union of its annotated rationale groups. Claims keep the dataset’s file order. Read requests carry at most 100 claims (200 questions, the API limit). For the reported conditions gpt-6-luna answered 400 scoring requests (5,880 sentence Booleans, 0 refused) and 1,809 read requests (50,733 claim answers and 50,733 sufficiency checks, 0 refused), with 20,142,083 input tokens. The data are available under the license terms of the Wikipedia article pages or, where unavailable, CC BY-SA 3.0.

sections.heading: Evidence Inference.
sections.text: Before any request of this experiment, we specified the corpus, the eligibility and sampling rules, a sample-size rule (the longest prefix of a seeded article order whose expected spend fits a fixed budget), the prompts, policies and budgets, the overlap definition, both hypotheses with their directions, tests and level, the estimand and the bootstrap seed, and which outcomes are exploratory, among them the evidence retention of Table 8 . The data are ERASER’s release ( DeYoung et al., 2020 ) of Evidence Inference ( Lehman et al., 2019 ) : full-text clinical-trial articles, one sentence per line, with prompts naming an intervention I I , a comparator C C and an outcome O O , a three-way label and annotated evidence sentences. Each prompt becomes the claim “Compared with C C , I I produced a statistically significant difference in O O .” The claim is true when the label is a significant increase or decrease and false for no significant difference (55% of the 3,707 claims are true; 112 sentences and 4.7 claims per article on average). The first prompt in file order is known; of the 2,915 hidden claims, 759 overlap the known claim’s evidence and 2,156 do not. Scoring and reading prompts are those of FEVER with the claim text substituted. gpt-6-luna answered 4,752 requests (34,695,247 input tokens, $3.47) with 37,070 read answers, of which 1 was a refusal. Both hypotheses are one-sided tests at nominal level 0.05 on 2000 article-bootstrap means of the paired typed − - random difference, each decided by the share of means on the wrong side of zero, with 50% as a secondary replication. H1 (overlapping claims, difference > 0 >0 ) is supported at both budgets (+21.4 points at 25%, +7.0 at 50%). H2 (disjoint claims, difference ≤ 0 \leq 0 ) is contradicted at both budgets: disjoint claims gain +9.8 [+7.4, +12.1] points at 25% and +3.9 [+2.0, +5.9] at 50%, and the share of bootstrap means at or below zero is < 0.0005 <0.0005 at each. Table 8 gives the exploratory unsplit contrast. Hidden accuracy at 25% is 92% (overlapping) and 80% (disjoint) under typed selection, 71% and 70% under random deletion, and 91% and 89% on the full text; the known claim is answered at 91%, 70% and 90%. sections.heading: Follow-up plan.
sections.text: One plan fixed four follow-ups with their comparisons, decision rules and budgets (A1–D2b). A: typed beats random deletion on the known question in every corpus, reader and budget (A1); on hidden MultiRC questions it is within ± \pm 2 points of random by the 90% interval, for each reader and budget (A2a); on hidden FEVER claims it beats random (A2b). B: if LongLLMLingua and MMR beat random on the known question and stay within the margin or below it on hidden questions, the MultiRC hidden result is attributed to conditioning on the known question. C1 and D0–D2b are stated with their results in Appendices J and M . Estimators and bootstrap units are the paper’s: document-macro accuracy, paired contrasts that drop an answer refused in either arm (on LoCoMo a refusal counts as wrong, as in Appendix M ), 2000 document resamples (conversations on LoCoMo). Random deletion at token budgets averages three seeded masks per document, computed as in Appendix C . Follow-ups A and B are reported here, C in Appendix J and D in Appendix M .

sections.heading: Token-matched budgets.
sections.text: A document’s budget is T = round ⁡ ( b ​ n ) T=\mathrm{round}(b\,n) tokens, where n n is the length of its full text under the tiktoken o200k_base encoding and b ∈ { 25 , 50 } % b\in\{25,50\}\% . A sentence policy adds whole sentences in its rank order while the count stays at most T T . It then cuts the first sentence that does not fit to the remaining tokens and stops; the pieces stay in document order. Typed and question-agnostic selection rank by the paper’s scores (on MultiRC, each reader by its own), TF-IDF selection by similarity to the known question, random deletion by a seeded permutation. For LLMLingua-2 and LongLLMLingua, the compression rate (or target length) is bisected to the smallest setting whose output reaches T T tokens, and the output is cut to T T . Every text is within 1 token of its target. LongLLMLingua ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) runs llmlingua 0.2.2 with Llama-2-7B as its scoring model, the sentences as contexts and the known question (or claim) as the query, with document order kept and the library’s settings otherwise. MMR ( Carbonell & Goldstein, 1998 ) ranks sentences greedily by 0.5 0.5 times the cosine to the query minus 0.5 0.5 times the largest cosine to a sentence already chosen, with bge-large-en-v1.5 embeddings ( Xiao et al., 2024 ) . Reads use the paper’s prompts: gpt-6-luna on MultiRC and FEVER and open-decider on MultiRC.

sections.heading: Appendix H Word-level compression: the granularity test and the hybrid
sections.text: LLMLingua-2 differs from random sentence deletion in two ways: it deletes words, so most sentences keep some words, and it chooses them by its scores. This experiment changes one at a time.

sections.heading: The known question.

With open-decider , typed selection is ahead at 50% (+3.5 [+1.0, +6.0] at matched tokens) and the 25% intervals span zero. On the known FEVER claim typed selection is ahead (+13.0 [+7.5, +18.5]).

sections.heading: Plan.
sections.text: The plan fixed the policies, contrasts, readers and budgets below and predicted at 25% that contrasts 1 (G1) and 2 (G2) are positive in each cell, with the interval above 0.

sections.heading: Policies.
sections.text: Every text has the token budget T T of Appendix G , to within 1 token. Four policies fill it: • Word scores : the LLMLingua-2 text of Appendix G . • Sentence scores : the same model, with no question. A word’s score is its keep probability in compress_prompt (the “preserve” probability averaged over its tokens), and a sentence’s score is the mean over its words. Sentences are added in descending score, ties in document order, as for the sentence policies of Appendix G . • Random words : whitespace-separated words are added in a seeded random order until the budget is reached, then kept in document order. Each document has three masks. • Random sentences : the random deletion of Appendix G , with its three masks. The four contrasts are (1) word scores − - sentence scores, (2) random words − - random sentences, (3) sentence scores − - random sentences and (4) word scores − - random words. Contrasts 1 and 2 change only the unit of deletion, contrasts 3 and 4 only whether the scores choose. Readers, prompts and estimators are those of Appendix G : paired, document-macro accuracy on hidden questions, with 2000 document resamples. A random policy’s value for a document is the mean over its three masks.

sections.heading: Appendix I Content-word evidence retention (exploratory)
sections.text: This analysis was not planned in advance and uses only the texts and reads of the hybrid experiment (Appendix H ); it sends no new request. A word is a content word if, lower-cased and stripped of surrounding punctuation, it contains a letter or digit and is not in scikit-learn’s English stop list. For each hidden question and compacted text we measure four shares. All words and content are the shares of its annotated evidence’s words and content words kept. Breadth is the share of its evidence sentences with at least one content word kept, and, on MultiRC, answer is the share of each candidate answer’s content words that occur in the kept text. The unit is one candidate answer (MultiRC) or claim (FEVER) in one compacted text, scored right or wrong, with refusals dropped and weights that make every document and policy count once. A linear probability model with document fixed effects and policy indicators pools the six policies of a cell; a feature enters as indicators of gold label by feature bin (0 and 1 are their own bins, interior values are cut at their pooled deciles) or, in the linear form, as one slope per gold label. The policy gap left after conditioning is the difference of policy coefficients, with 2000 document-bootstrap resamples. The FEVER evidence-support check of Section 4 uses the binary reads. A claim’s target is “supported” if it is true and its evidence is fully kept (all evidence sentences for sentence policies, all evidence content words for word policies), “not supported” if its evidence is entirely deleted, and undefined otherwise; accuracy weights the two targets equally. Unlike the three-way target of Appendix J , it leaves a false claim with fully kept evidence undefined, so the FEVER typed − - random contrast covers fewer claims (3,685 against 4,528). The label split of Section 4 covers 3,850 true and 1,582 false hidden claims; the bin with at most a fifth of the evidence content words kept holds 458 true claims after LLMLingua-2 and 2,575 after random sentence deletion; the target is defined for 45 of the 5,432 hidden claims answered under LLMLingua-2 (one claim refused there is dropped), for 3,685 claims in the typed − - random contrast and for 1,140 in the hybrid − - typed contrast. The relaxed variant counts evidence as kept above 80% and as deleted below 20% of its content words; under it LLMLingua-2 − - random sentence deletion is − - 19.8 [ − - 29.7 , − - 12.0 ] points on the 675 claims where both texts define it. Table 15 gives the gaps at 25%. Content-word retention lowers every gap and leaves no detected LLMLingua-2 − - random-sentence gap on FEVER. Breadth alone over-corrects: conditioning on it turns several gaps negative, because random word deletion also keeps some word of most evidence sentences yet scores lower. On FEVER the all-word measure, binned, also absorbs most of the LLMLingua-2 gap, because the relation between FEVER accuracy and retention is strongly non-linear; in the linear form content-word retention leaves +14.9 points there, so on FEVER the two measures are not separated. sections.heading: Appendix K The prespecified KEEP–DROP contrast
sections.text: Before any request of this experiment, we specified the corpora, the two arms, the reader and prompt, the size-based exclusion, the estimand, the bootstrap seeds, both predictions with their test and level, and which outcomes are descriptive. Only item construction and token counting, which use sentence sets alone, came first.

sections.heading: Design.
sections.text: The sample is every document already read under typed selection at 25%: 200 FEVER documents and 792 Evidence Inference articles. Let K K be typed selection’s kept set, k = | K | k=|K| , and E E the union of a hidden claim’s annotated rationale groups. KEEP is K K with E ∖ K E\setminus K added and as many sentences of K ∖ E K\setminus E removed, lowest typed-selection score first; DROP is K K with K ∩ E K\cap E removed and as many sentences drawn uniformly (seeded per claim) from outside K ∪ E K\cup E added. Both have k k sentences in document order; KEEP holds all of E E and DROP none of it, and when K K already holds all of E E (or none), KEEP (or DROP) is K K itself. Sentences swapped in or out may be evidence for other claims, so the two arms can differ in more than the claim’s evidence. Averaged over the analyzed hidden claims (a claim mean, unlike the retention shares of Table 8 ), K K already holds 49% of a hidden claim’s evidence on FEVER and 57% on Evidence Inference. gpt-6-luna answers one claim per request with the claim and sufficiency checks of the main reads, worded as before; a claim counts as correct when its probability is on the side of its gold label. All 16,102 requests were sent as one shuffled list, so arms and corpora are interleaved in time (15,135,563 input tokens, $1.51).

sections.heading: KEEP beats DROP.
sections.text: At the last checkpoint, gpt-6-luna answers a hidden question more accurately from the typed 25% memory with its evidence (KEEP) than from one with the same number of turns without it (DROP). KEEP − - DROP is +13.3 points, positive in all 10 conversations, on all questions and on the 1,408 evidence-disjoint ones, so H2a and H2b are supported. Read by qwen3.8-flash , the same texts also meet H2’s decision rule (+10.7 [+8.3, +13.3] on all questions). The four options include no “not supported” answer, so missing evidence cannot make the reader right by default.

sections.heading: Typed versus random deletion is unresolved at 25%.
sections.text: With empty memory at 81.4%, absolute differences are small. H1, typed − - random hidden accuracy at 25%, is unresolved for both readers, and so is the typed − - random difference in evidence kept. H3, which asks the first to follow the second, therefore cannot be assessed. H4 is supported: low sufficiency ranks hidden questions with dropped evidence first (AUROC 0.81 [0.79, 0.84]). Question-agnostic selection keeps more of hidden questions’ evidence turns than typed selection (48.6% against 27.2% at 25%), but also longer turns (Appendix L ). With harder answer options, in a prespecified follow-up, KEEP still beats DROP and typed versus random stays unresolved (Table 20 ).

sections.heading: Plan, data and cost.
sections.text: Before any request of this experiment, we specified the data, checkpoints, known-question rule, policies, read format, readers, the four hypotheses with their tests, the bootstrap seed and the outcomes reported without a decision rule. Only item construction and token estimation (no model answer) came first. The data are locomo10.json from the authors’ repository ( Maharana et al., 2024 ) at commit 3eb6f2c , released under CC BY-NC 4.0; our use is non-commercial research, and we use the released photo captions as text. gpt-6-luna cost $5.08 (50,816,715 input tokens) and qwen3.8-flash $12.10 (80,631,483 prompt tokens).

sections.heading: Design.
sections.text: Eligible questions are LoCoMo’s categories 1–4 (multi-hop, temporal, open-domain, single-hop) with a gold answer and at least one valid evidence turn, 1,536 in all; adversarial questions have no gold answer. Memory is rendered as session blocks, each headed by its session’s date, then one line per kept turn with its speaker and any photo caption. Headers do not count against the budget, since temporal answers are relative to session dates. With S S sessions, checkpoint k k closes session ⌈ k ​ S / 4 ⌉ \lceil kS/4\rceil . The known question at k k is, among unused eligible questions whose last evidence turn lies in segment k k , the one with the smallest CRC32 checksum of a fixed key. At checkpoint k k with N k N_{k} turns seen, a policy keeps round ⁡ ( b ​ N k ) \mathrm{round}(bN_{k}) of the previous memory plus the new turns, and a dropped turn never returns. Typed and agnostic use gpt-6-luna scores with the known- and agnostic-policy wording of the earlier corpora, “sentence” replaced by “turn”; TF-IDF, random and lead are as before, recency keeps the latest turns. Hidden questions at k k are every eligible question whose evidence lies before checkpoint k k , except the conversation’s four known questions: 351, 671, 1,061 and 1,496 at k = 1 , … , 4 k=1,\dots,4 . The three distractors of a question are answers to other questions of the same conversation, same category first, with near-duplicates excluded and the option order fixed by a hash. gpt-6-luna reads up to 100 questions per request, each with the Choice and the sufficiency check (“does the conversation memory contain the information needed to answer this question?”). qwen3.8-flash answers one question per call from first-token log-probabilities over the option letters (thinking off), at the last checkpoint, for typed, TF-IDF, random and recency at 25%, full and empty memory, on gpt-6-luna ’s selections. A refusal counts as wrong; dropping instead every question refused under either memory condition of a contrast changes no planned decision.

sections.heading: Tests.
sections.text: Every estimate is the mean over conversations of the per-conversation mean paired difference, with 2000 conversation-bootstrap resamples. H1 (two-sided) is positive or negative if the 95% interval excludes zero and unresolved otherwise; H2a and H2b (one-sided, nominal level 0.05) are supported if the 5th percentile is above zero. KEEP is the typed 25% memory at the last checkpoint with the question’s missing evidence added and as many non-evidence turns removed, lowest typed score first. DROP removes its kept evidence and adds as many turns drawn at random from outside the memory and the evidence. Each of the 2,992 KEEP and DROP reads asks one question, in one shuffled list. H3 is consistent or inconsistent only if H1 and the typed − - random retention difference are both resolved. H4 is supported if the 2.5th percentile of a conversation bootstrap of the pooled AUROC exceeds 0.5. With ten clusters the percentile bootstrap may under-cover. Pooled over questions, KEEP scores 97.7% and DROP 85.1%.

sections.heading: Test results.
sections.text: H1, typed − - random at 25%, is − - 0.4 [ − - 2.1 , +1.0 ] with gpt-6-luna and +0.6 [ − - 1.8 , +2.8 ] with qwen3.8-flash , both unresolved. KEEP − - DROP is +13.3 [ +10.9 , +16.4 ] on all hidden questions (H2a, supported) and +13.3 [ +10.7 , +16.8 ] on evidence-disjoint ones (H2b, supported). The conversation-macro typed − - random difference in evidence kept is +2.1 [ − - 2.5 , +6.5 ], so H3 is not assessable. The sufficiency AUROC against dropped evidence is 0.81 [0.79, 0.84] (H4, supported).

sections.heading: Second reader.
sections.text: In the plan qwen3.8-flash reads six memory conditions to replicate H1; its KEEP–DROP reads are an exploratory extension under H2’s decision rule. qwen3.8-flash read the same 1,496 KEEP and DROP pairs, one question per call, with no refusals. KEEP − - DROP is +10.7 [+8.3, +13.3] points on all questions (90.8% vs. 80.5%; 5th percentile +8.6), +10.6 [+8.0, +13.3] on the 1,408 disjoint ones (5th percentile +8.5) and +9.1 [+4.1, +15.2] on the 88 overlapping ones, positive in 10, 10 and 6 of ten conversations. Both 5th percentiles are above zero, so the H2a and H2b rules are also met on this reader. The accuracies in parentheses are question-pooled and the contrasts conversation-macro, so they need not subtract exactly.

sections.heading: Harder options (follow-up D).
sections.text: With harder options, empty memory drops to 60.2% ( gpt-6-luna ) and 71.5% ( qwen3.8-flash ; Table 20 ). Only the three wrong options of each question change; questions, memories and KEEP/DROP texts are those of Section 5 . For temporal questions and questions asking how many, how long or when, the wrong options are the gold answer with its date shifted by one to four weeks (same month first) or its number shifted (21.1% of wrong options). Otherwise they are answers to questions of the same form (same head noun or opening words), ranked by TF-IDF similarity of the questions. They come from other conversations if they name no speaker (59.5%), or from the same conversation if their question is not a near duplicate (17.0%). Yes/no answers keep the original options (2.3%). The plan set a target of at most 60% question-pooled empty-memory accuracy for gpt-6-luna . The construction reaches a question-pooled 60.2% (original options 82.2%), missing the target by 0.2 points. Table 20 gives, per memory and reader, the refusal rate, the accuracy over all questions (refusals wrong) and the accuracy over answered questions. Full-memory accuracy falls to 90.9% (original options: 96.8%), since a shifted date can be hard to rule out even with the whole conversation. The plan applies the rules of H1 (D1) and H2a and H2b (D2a, D2b). Typed − - random at 25% is +1.3 [ − - 1.7, +4.3] ( gpt-6-luna ) and +0.2 [ − - 2.9, +3.2] ( qwen3.8-flash ), unresolved. KEEP − - DROP is +18.5 [+15.6, +21.3] and +14.7 [+10.7, +18.8], and on evidence-disjoint questions +18.7 [ +15.8 , +21.5 ] and +15.1, supported for both readers. Dropping refused answers (exploratory) leaves every decision unchanged.

sections.heading: Typed selection beats random deletion on hidden questions.
sections.text: Typed − - random is +22.3 [ +15.1 , +28.9 ] points with gpt-6-luna and +21.7 [ +15.7 , +27.6 ] with qwen3.8-flash (Table 21 ), unlike on MultiRC. Typed selection also keeps the hidden question’s identifier more often (66.4% against 42.4%), and hidden questions whose identifier survives score 85.9%, against 18.9% when it is lost. This association is consistent with the relation between gain and evidence kept of Section 3 . LLMLingua-2 keeps the identifier for 52.3% and shows no detected gain ( +4.0 [ − - 1.1 , +9.3 ]). Recency, which keeps the newest units, gains +9.1 points on hidden questions but scores only 28.9% on the known one, because the identifiers sit in earlier units.

sections.heading: Anticipating later calls costs the known question.
sections.text: ECov − - typed is +12.8 [ +5.2 , +20.8 ] on hidden questions but − - 10.6 (90% interval [ − - 17.8, − - 2.9]) on the known one; anticipatory selection gives +8.7 and − - 12.0. No selector we tested beats typed selection on both. Fetching dropped units on demand also stays well below the full state at about the same passage tokens (recoverable arm below).

sections.heading: Sample and questions.
sections.text: The trajectories are the successful (reward 1) retail trajectories of the two agents whose histories τ \tau -bench releases (MIT license); airline trajectories (41 states) are descriptive only: gpt-6-luna scores 76.7% (full), 66.8% (typed), 60.0% (random) and 27.2% (empty) on its hidden questions. The plan, with its predictions, was written before any request. The 40 pilot trajectories were inspected to choose the newest-first tie-break of anticipatory selection and are excluded. The checkpoint is the middle tool output. Questions whose gold identifier is ambiguous, not identifier-like or a bare list entry are dropped, and in quoted text every substring with the gold’s character pattern is masked. In six retail hidden questions a later user turn gives the identifier without its leading “#”, which this mask misses; dropping them moves typed − - random and LLMLingua-2 − - random by at most 0.2 points. A known question exists when the next call’s identifier argument occurs in the state with at least one same-shaped distractor (407 known questions, one per identifier argument of the next call). A refusal counts as wrong; the full-state refusal rate is 1.9% (95% upper limit 2.9%), so the prespecified validity check passes. Other arms refuse more often (retail, gpt-6-luna ): random 16.0%, LLMLingua-2 16.2%, typed 10.9%, anticipatory 6.4%, ECov 6.9% and empty 66.7%. On answered questions only, typed − - random is +23.0 [ +17.4 , +27.8 ], LLMLingua-2 − - random +4.0 [ − - 1.2 , +8.9 ], ECov − - typed +5.8 [ − - 1.4 , +13.6 ], anticipatory − - typed +2.9 [ − - 1.5 , +8.0 ] and recency − - random +4.4 [ − - 1.8 , +11.2 ] points on hidden questions.

sections.heading: Selectors.
sections.text: Budgets are T = round ( 0.25 × T=\mathrm{round}(0.25\times the state’s o200k tokens ) ) , filled unit by unit in rank order. Typed selection ranks units by gpt-6-luna ’s probability that the unit is needed for the known question; typed, newest-first breaks its ties toward newer units. ECov adds units greedily by their gain in F ⁡ ( S ) = ∑ q w q ​ [ 1 − ∏ u ∈ S ( 1 − p ⁡ ( u , q ) ) ] F(S)=\sum_{q}w_{q}\,[1-\prod_{u\in S}(1-p(u,q))] , with weight 0.5 on the known question ( p p = the typed probability) and 0.05 on each of the ten generated questions ( p p from a gpt-6-luna Boolean per unit and question). ECov-embed replaces the latter by a logistic function of the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 cosine between unit and question. Hybrid keeps typed whole units up to half the budget and fills the rest with LLMLingua-2 words. Gist writes every unit as a numbered line holding its top LLMLingua-2 words within 60% of the budget, then restores typed whole units. Table 21 gives these arms; their predictions are under Prespecified predictions below. Under recency the newest unit takes a median 8.5% of the budget, and the rest of its budget goes to the next-newest units.

sections.heading: Recoverable arm.
sections.text: Dropped units leave either a stub naming the run of dropped units and their roles, or the gist line above, so each unit keeps its position. A hidden question whose sufficiency is below a threshold θ \theta is re-read alone with dropped units added in order of TF-IDF match between the question and what remains visible of them, up to a quarter of the full state’s tokens. With gists at θ = 0.5 \theta=0.5 it reaches 69.1% against 88.8% for the full state, at 102.0% of the full state’s passage tokens (o200k, without the question and option text) per question (Table 22 ). Low sufficiency ranks questions whose identifier was dropped first (AUROC 0.73 with stubs, 0.72 with gists), so the main failure is choosing the units to fetch. The first pass reads all questions of a state plus the sufficiency check (Section 3 ) for each hidden question; it scores 64.0% on hidden questions with stubs and 51.3% with gists. Tokens per question count the first read divided by the state’s hidden questions, plus the re-read. Table 22 gives question-mean accuracy; the full state scores 88.8% on the same questions. We evaluate compaction on these later questions, using four corpora that annotate the evidence of several questions per text and recorded agent trajectories, and compare every method with random deletion at the same budget. On MultiRC, keeping the sentences that gpt-6-luna (through the OpenAI Decisions API) judges necessary for the current question raises its accuracy on that question by 11.4 points at 25% of the tokens. On the later questions, however, no method that selects sentences for the current question does detectably better than deleting sentences at random. Deleting words instead of sentences does better: LLMLingua-2 , which ignores the question, beats random sentence deletion at the same token count by 12.5 points on the later MultiRC questions. It keeps about twice random deletion’s share of the evidence’s content words, and at equal content-word retention its gain shrinks to 7.3 points (exploratory). On FEVER, label accuracy can overstate what the kept text supports: the gain of sentence selection is no longer detected when answers are scored against the kept evidence, and the 21.0-point gain of LLMLingua-2 is not shown to rest on the kept text. The ranking also depends on the setting: on Evidence Inference sentence selection beats LLMLingua-2 at a nominal 25% budget, and on τ \tau -bench trajectories, whose later tool calls need exact identifiers, it beats random deletion while LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain. Scores on the question a compaction was made for do not reliably show how it serves later ones. † † footnotetext: AI assistance: The authors used Claude Code (Anthropic) during the preparation of this work. 1 Introduction Applications that call a language model many times, such as agents, assistants and multi-step pipelines, carry text from one call to the next: documents read so far, conversation turns, tool outputs. We call this text the state . Every call pays for it in tokens and the context window bounds it, so applications compact it: they delete parts of it to fit a budget. At compaction time the application usually knows its current question, and the natural choice is to keep what that question needs. The state, however, outlives that question. Later questions, unknown when the deletion was made, must be answered from whatever survived, and a deleted sentence is gone for all of them. We call the question available at compaction time known and the later ones hidden . Query-aware compressors are usually evaluated on the question they compress for; we evaluate them on the hidden ones. We compare query-aware selection, which keeps what the known question needs, with question-agnostic compressors. Our main instance uses typed decision models , which take a state and typed questions about it (a Boolean, a Choice among options or a Score) and return a probability for each answer ( TypeSafe AI, 2026 ; OpenAI, 2026 ) . Typed selection asks one Boolean per sentence, “is this sentence needed to answer the question?”, and keeps the most probable sentences; the same model then answers the questions, and in this role we call it the reader . Figure 1 shows the risk. We compare it with random deletion, question-agnostic selection by the same model, TF-IDF (term frequency–inverse document frequency) selection and lead (the first sentences). We also run LLMLingua-2 ( Pan et al., 2024 ) , which deletes individual words without any question, and, at token budgets, LongLLMLingua ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) and maximal marginal relevance (MMR; Carbonell & Goldstein, 1998 ), two established compressors that use the question. The corpora are MultiRC ( Khashabi et al., 2018 ; Wang et al., 2019 ) , ERASER’s FEVER ( Thorne et al., 2018 ; DeYoung et al., 2020 ) , Evidence Inference ( Lehman et al., 2019 ) and LoCoMo conversation memory ( Maharana et al., 2024 ) , in which several questions share one text and each question’s evidence is annotated, and recorded τ \tau -bench agent trajectories ( Yao et al., 2024 ) , whose questions ask for the identifiers that later tool calls pass. Our findings are: • Selection for the known question beats random deletion on that question. On MultiRC, typed selection, MMR and LongLLMLingua raise known-question accuracy over random deletion at 25%, but none shows a detected advantage on hidden questions on average. On MultiRC, hidden questions gain only where they share the known question’s evidence. On FEVER, a gain in recovering a claim’s label is not detected when the kept text is scored for what it supports (Section 3 ). The label-accuracy gain of word-level compression there is not shown to rest on the kept text either (Section 4 ). • On MultiRC, picking words beats picking sentences by the same scores. With the same importance scores, picking words instead of sentences raises hidden-question accuracy, and LLMLingua-2 and a hybrid of typed sentences and LLMLingua-2 words lead on hidden questions. They keep about as many evidence words as random deletion but far more of the evidence’s content words, which partly explains the lead: at equal content-word retention it shrinks from 12.5 to 7.3 points with gpt-6-luna (Section 4 ). • The ordering is not stable across settings. On Evidence Inference typed selection beats LLMLingua-2 on hidden claims at a nominal 25% budget. On agent trajectories, whose later calls need exact identifiers, typed selection beats random deletion and LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain (Section 5 ). Concurrent work shows that compaction can serve the current query and fail later ones ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Zhang, 2026 ) . We add an evaluation on annotated evidence that compares sentence- and word-level compression and locates where each serves later questions. 2 Evaluation setup This section describes the MultiRC experiment; Sections 3 and 5 give the changes for the other settings. Data and models. Each MultiRC question has several candidate answers that annotators labeled correct or incorrect, and a question can have more than one correct answer. We use 300 paragraphs with at least three questions and 6–20 sentences, with 3,355 questions and 17,895 candidate answers, from the validation and training splits (validation alone has too few such paragraphs). The first listed question of each paragraph is known and the others are hidden. gpt-6-luna reads every corpus. Every gpt-6-luna read and selection in this paper goes through the OpenAI Decisions API ( OpenAI, 2026 ) , the typed decision interface: a request poses typed questions and returns a probability for each answer, with no generated text. Three open-weight models built for the typed decision interface, open-decider (2B), open-bosun (1.7B) and open-lumma (0.6B) ( Mapika, 2026 ; Hanno Labs, 2026 ; FrontiersMind, 2026 ) , also read MultiRC from their released weights, and qwen3.8-flash is a general instruction-tuned reader (Appendix B ). We drop refused answers; counting them as wrong instead changes neither the sign of any typed − - random contrast nor whether its interval excludes zero (Appendix B ). Selectors and budgets. Both model-based selectors ask one Boolean per sentence, with the sentences numbered in the state. Typed selection puts the known question in the state and asks “is sentence i i needed to answer the question?”. Question-agnostic selection gives no question and asks “does sentence i i state a fact that a reader is likely to be asked about later?”. A policy keeps a budget b ∈ { 25 , 50 , 75 } % b\in\{25,50,75\}\% of a paragraph’s sentences (rounded half to even, at least one). Typed and agnostic selection keep the most probable sentences, TF-IDF selection those closest to the known question, lead the first ones, and random deletion one seeded uniform sample. Kept sentences stay in document order. Token-matched tests cut every text, LLMLingua-2 ’s included, to the same o200k token count (Appendix G ). Reading and measures. One request asks one Boolean per candidate answer: “given the passage, is this a correct answer to the question?”, where “no” is defined as “not supported or incorrect”. Once a compaction deletes the evidence for a correct answer, the reader is therefore asked to reject that answer. We score each candidate answer against the MultiRC labels, average within each paragraph, then over paragraphs, with paragraph-bootstrap 95% intervals; a difference is detected when its interval excludes zero. Answering “no” to every candidate already scores 55.6%, and of the four typed readers only gpt-6-luna (88.2%) and open-decider (75.3%) are detectably above it on the full text, so the main tables report these two. A hidden question is overlapping if its annotated evidence shares a sentence with the known question’s, and disjoint otherwise. Prespecified analyses. Hypotheses, tests and decision rules were specified before any model request for the Evidence Inference overlap test, the KEEP–DROP contrast, the LoCoMo test and four follow-ups under one plan (token-matched budgets, query-aware baselines, three-way labels and harder LoCoMo options). The same holds for the LLMLingua-2 granularity test, the hybrid compactor, a test with a different known question, a general-reader test, the τ \tau -bench test and the abstractive-summary test. Appendix A counts the outcomes and lists every prediction that was not fully met. The other analyses, including the content-word analysis and the FEVER evidence-support check of Section 4 , are exploratory. Deleted evidence drives the losses. A hidden answer that was right on the full text flips more often when its evidence was deleted. With gpt-6-luna , adding some of the deleted evidence back undoes more flips than adding as many sentences that are evidence for no question ( +26.8 [ +22.6 , +31.5 ] points; Appendix D ). A sufficiency check (“does the passage contain the information needed to answer this question?”) ranks questions with broken evidence first. Yet re-reading a random quarter of hidden questions on the full text recovers most of what re-reading the lowest-sufficiency quarter does (Appendix D ). FEVER and Evidence Inference: hidden claims gain in label recovery. Each question here is a claim, and the reader judges whether the text supports it. We sample 200 FEVER documents with 5,433 hidden claims and 792 Evidence Inference clinical-trial articles (Appendix E ); the first claim of each document is known. On FEVER at 25% typed − - random hidden-claim accuracy is +17.2 points, and on Evidence Inference disjoint claims gain too, with more of their evidence kept than random deletion keeps (Figure 2 ). Label recovery and support scoring disagree. Label accuracy counts the document’s label as right even when a claim’s evidence was deleted. A prespecified three-way read therefore also scores each answer against what the kept text supports: the document’s label if all of the claim’s annotated evidence was kept and “not enough info” if all of it was deleted. In this read, with true and false claims weighted equally, typed selection on FEVER recovers the label 25.2 points more often than random deletion, while its support-target accuracy, with the three targets weighted equally, differs from random deletion by − - 1.0 [ − - 3.9 , +2.2 ] points (Appendix J ). Prespecified KEEP–DROP tests give a hidden claim two texts with the same number of sentences, one with its evidence and one without; KEEP beats DROP by +50.0 [ +47.4 , +52.4 ] points on FEVER and +17.8 [ +15.9 , +19.7 ] on Evidence Inference (Appendix K ). For sentence selection, the gain follows the extra evidence kept. Across the eight 25% groups of Figure 2 (corpus, reader, overlapping or disjoint), the typed − - random hidden gain rises with how much more of the hidden questions’ evidence typed selection keeps than random deletion, at 0.37 0.37 points of gain per point of extra evidence. We fixed this line before a second experiment that repeats typed selection with a different, randomly drawn known question in every document. On the eight new groups it misses the observed gains by 3.4 points on average.
