LLMLingua-2 is also ahead of typed selection on hidden questions in all three cells (Table 2 ). The hybrid beats typed selection on hidden questions in all three cells, by 4.6 to 8.3 points with every interval above zero; it beats LLMLingua-2 on FEVER and stays below it on MultiRC (Appendix H ). The gain comes from picking words. A prespecified test keeps the LLMLingua-2 scores and changes only the unit kept. Picking words instead of whole sentences raises hidden-question accuracy at 25% by +11.7 points (MultiRC, gpt-6-luna ), +4.6 (MultiRC, open-decider ) and +19.1 (FEVER). Whole sentences picked by the same scores are not detectably better than random sentence deletion in five of six cells (Appendix H ). On the known MultiRC question LLMLingua-2 is ahead of typed selection with gpt-6-luna in all four comparisons. The two intervals at sentence budgets exclude zero, and the one at 50% of the tokens just does (upper end − 0.02 -0.02 points) (Appendices G and H ). Word-level compression keeps the evidence’s content words. Counted over all words, LLMLingua-2 , the hybrid and random sentence deletion keep similar shares of the hidden questions’ evidence on MultiRC, yet their accuracies differ by up to 12.5 points. Sentence deletion keeps a sentence’s content and function words together. LLMLingua-2 drops function words first, so it keeps 48.0% of the evidence’s content words against 26.1% for random sentence deletion (Table 2 ). For sentence policies the two counts agree within half a point, so the relation of Section 3 is unchanged. Content-word retention accounts for part of the lead. A model of each answer’s correctness, with document fixed effects, compares policies at equal content-word retention. It describes an association, since the policies produce the retention they are compared at. At equal retention the MultiRC LLMLingua-2 − - random-sentence gap shrinks from 12.5 to +7.3 [ +6.1 , +8.4 ] points with gpt-6-luna and from 6.0 to +2.0 [ +0.7 , +3.2 ] with open-decider . Also conditioning on how many of each candidate answer’s content words survive leaves +4.9 points with gpt-6-luna and +0.6 [ − - 0.5 , +1.8 ] with open-decider . The hybrid − - typed gaps shrink the same way (Table 15 ). On FEVER binned retention leaves 1.3 points; a linear term leaves 14.9, because accuracy rises non-linearly with retention there. Which words are kept matters too. On FEVER typed selection keeps more of the hidden claims’ content words than LLMLingua-2 yet scores lower (Table 2 ). At the same content-word retention LLMLingua-2 still beats random word deletion by +6.7 [ +5.5 , +8.0 ] points on MultiRC with gpt-6-luna , +1.7 [ +0.5 , +2.9 ] with open-decider and +9.6 [ +7.5 , +11.7 ] on FEVER (Appendix I ). LLM-written summaries stay below word-level compression. A compaction can also have an LLM rewrite the text. Two summarizers, qwen3.8-flash and gpt-6.1-sol , summarized each MultiRC paragraph within the same token budget, once for unknown later questions and once for the known question (Appendix O ). On hidden questions the generic summaries beat random sentence deletion by 7.6 and 10.9 points but stay below LLMLingua-2 : summary − - LLMLingua-2 is − - 4.5 [ − - 5.7 , − - 3.2 ] and − - 1.3 [ − - 2.4 , − - 0.3 ] points. The summaries written for the known question answer it better than typed selection and LLMLingua-2 (88.5% and 89.2%), but on hidden questions they fall below random deletion ( qwen3.8-flash , − - 2.9 [ − - 4.0 , − - 1.8 ]) or show no detected gain ( gpt-6.1-sol , +0.9 [ − - 0.2 , +2.1 ]). On FEVER, label accuracy overstates the word-level gain. FEVER accuracy counts the document’s label, which Section 3 shows can be right without textual support. The LLMLingua-2 gain over random sentence deletion lies on true claims ( +31.5 [ +28.0 , +35.0 ] points; false claims − - 2.2 [ − - 3.7 , − - 1.0 ]). When at most a fifth of a true claim’s evidence content words survive, the reader still calls it supported for 56.0% of claims after LLMLingua-2 and 26.8% after random sentence deletion. An evidence-support target, scored on the binary reads, reproduces the three-way result for typed − - random ( − - 0.2 [ − - 3.4 , +3.0 ] points, label-balanced) and removes the hybrid’s gain over typed selection ( − - 3.7 [ − - 9.4 , +1.3 ]). Under LLMLingua-2 it is undefined for 99% of hidden claims, whose evidence is partly kept, so its FEVER gain is not shown to rest on the kept text (Appendix I ). 5 The ordering is not stable: Evidence Inference and agent states Evidence Inference. On Evidence Inference typed selection keeps more of even the disjoint claims’ evidence than random deletion (Figure 2 ). It beats LLMLingua-2 on hidden claims when LLMLingua-2 is set to the compression rate of 25% sentence deletion ( +12.2 [ +10.1 , +14.4 ] points); at the 50% rate the difference is +1.0 [ − - 0.5 , +2.6 ]. This comparison is not token-matched: at 25% the typed texts keep 28.9% of the article’s o200k tokens and the LLMLingua-2 texts 25.8% (Appendices G and L ). Agent trajectories. In the recorded τ \tau -bench retail trajectories an agent calls tools for a simulated user. The state is a trajectory up to its middle tool output, split into turns, tool calls and tool outputs. The known question asks which identifier (an order, item, product or payment-method ID, or a zip code) the next tool call passes; each hidden question asks the same for a later call, among same-shaped identifiers from the state. On 390 states with 837 hidden questions at 25% of the tokens, typed − - random is +22.3 [ +15.1 , +28.9 ] points with gpt-6-luna and +21.7 [ +15.7 , +27.6 ] with qwen3.8-flash , while LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain ( +4.0 [ − - 1.1 , +9.3 ]); token-level extractive compressors are known to strip the action syntax that agents need ( Zhang & Sun, 2026 ) . Typed selection keeps the hidden question’s identifier for 66.4% of hidden questions against 42.4% (random) and 52.3% ( LLMLingua-2 ). Anticipating later calls costs the known one. Selectors that anticipate later calls trade the known call for the hidden ones: on a 120-state subsample, expected-coverage selection gains +12.8 [ +5.2 , +20.8 ] points over typed selection on hidden questions and − - 10.6 (90% interval [ − - 17.8, − - 2.9]) on the known one. About half of the hidden gain comes from fewer refusals: scored on answered questions only, it is +5.8 [ − - 1.4 , +13.6 ] (Appendix N ). Conversation memory. LoCoMo’s ten long conversations are compacted four times as they grow, so a dropped turn never returns. At the last checkpoint, a typed 25% memory with a hidden question’s evidence beats one with the same number of turns without it by 13.3 points ( gpt-6-luna ), in all 10 conversations. Typed versus random deletion is unresolved for both readers, and on the four-choice format empty memory already scores 81.4% (Appendix M ). 6 Discussion Query-aware sentence selection raises the known question’s accuracy over random deletion. On later questions it helps those that share the known question’s evidence. On MultiRC, where many do not, it does no better than random deletion on average. On MultiRC the compressors that lead on later questions delete words. They drop function words first, so the same token budget holds more of the evidence’s content words. At equal content-word retention two fifths to two thirds of LLMLingua-2 ’s MultiRC lead over random sentence deletion disappears, and LLMLingua-2 still beats random words, so which words are kept also matters. On FEVER, typed selection’s label gain is not detected under support scoring, and the word-level gain is not shown to rest on the kept text. The ordering is not general. On Evidence Inference, where even disjoint claims keep more evidence under typed selection, it beats LLMLingua-2 at a nominal 25% budget. On agent trajectories, whose later calls need exact identifiers, LLMLingua-2 keeps fewer of them than typed selection and shows no detected gain. For evaluation, the results suggest scoring hidden questions as well as the known one, comparing with random deletion at matched tokens, measuring the hidden questions’ evidence kept in content words, and reporting support-based scoring next to label recovery. Compaction also costs tokens to build: for typed selection at 25% with gpt-6-luna , compacting once pays for itself in input tokens only with one request per later question, after about 6.6 to 11.0 of them on FEVER, Evidence Inference and LoCoMo. On Evidence Inference this is more than its mean of 3.7 later questions, and on MultiRC the extrapolated break-even, 14.0, exceeds its mean of 10.2 (Appendix L ). Keeping the full state allows a re-read for a later question, but neither recovery we tested matches it. On MultiRC, re-reading the lowest-sufficiency quarter of hidden questions on the full text lifts accuracy over all hidden questions from 67% to 74%, against 89% on the full text (Appendix D ). On agent trajectories, fetching dropped units on demand reaches 69.1% against 88.8% for the full state at 102.0% of its passage tokens, and the prespecified prediction that it would come close is not met (Appendix N ). 7 Related work Prompt compression removes tokens or sentences by perplexity ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) , by query-aware importance ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) or by a learned task-agnostic importance ( Pan et al., 2024 ) , and key–value (KV) cache compression has the same split ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . Earlier agent-memory work studied the same write-before-query asymmetry. TierMem ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) falls back to a raw log when a router judges pre-query summaries insufficient, and EMBER ( Li et al., 2026 ) learns which evidence to retain before the query. Chen et al. (2026) find that query-aware KV eviction does not generalize across queries, and Yu et al. (2026) separate write-time from retrieval-time loss. We delete sentences (turns on LoCoMo) for one known question and test the questions hidden at deletion time with annotated evidence and KEEP–DROP substitutions. The closest work is concurrent. Tirmazi et al. (2026) formalize compaction against later queries, with a set-membership case study, and Liu et al. (2026) find that compacting agent KV caches before later queries arrive hurts, and that deferring compaction recovers much of the cost; RestoreKV ( Baek et al., 2026 ) adds learned restoration to query-agnostic eviction, and Luo et al. (2026) find that hiding the question at compression time reorders KV-cache compressors, with most no better than trivial baselines. These work on KV caches rather than on evidence-annotated text. Liu (2026) counts the extra retrieval calls an agent makes to re-acquire state that compression dropped, and Zhang (2026) tests whether compressed memory keeps what a later update needs on synthetic histories; we measure answer accuracy on later questions of existing corpora and locate the loss with evidence annotations. Wang et al. (2026) find that context compactors keep about a sixth of the constraints a user sets for the agent’s later behavior. Sadowski & Chudziak (2026) and Shen & Li (2026) optimize what is written when the later goal is known. Mnemon ( Wang, 2026 ) uses the same per-record “is this needed” Boolean but keeps its raw records recoverable. Shankaranarayana et al. (2026) find that asking whether the evidence suffices is more informative than answer confidence; we ask it after compaction has deleted part of the evidence. Ai et al. (2026) find that KV-cache eviction can keep final-answer accuracy while the reasoning that supports the answer degrades; on FEVER we find the analogous gap between label accuracy and the evidence the kept text retains. 8 Limitations The experiments use public text and conversation benchmarks and recorded agent trajectories, not live agents. Abstractive summaries are tested only on MultiRC at a 25% budget. In the τ \tau -bench test the actions and tool outputs are fixed by the recording, the questions ask only for identifiers, retail is the only domain with enough trajectories for inference, and the only budget is 25%. The relation between gain and evidence kept is tested by consistency across settings, KEEP–DROP interventions and one out-of-sample check on the three document corpora, for sentence selection; it could not be assessed on LoCoMo and holds only qualitatively on τ \tau -bench. The content-word analysis of word-level compression is exploratory, leaves part of the MultiRC gap unexplained and, on FEVER, does not separate content words from all words. The model-based sentence selectors are typed models, which usually also answer; qwen3.8-flash is the only general instruction-tuned reader, and it reads the texts that gpt-6-luna selected. Only two typed readers perform above the all-“no” baseline on MultiRC. On the three document corpora the known question is the first listed one or, in one test, one other randomly drawn question per document. Evidence annotations are incomplete, so neither the retention tests nor the evidence-support target can account for unannotated evidence. Budgets count sentences or conversation turns, except in the token-matched tests and the τ \tau -bench test; Appendix L counts input tokens. The KEEP–DROP comparison covers one budget and does not include MultiRC. LoCoMo has ten conversations and a four-choice format on which empty memory already scores 81.4%. Hosted reads taken at different times can differ slightly (Appendix C ). Intervals are unadjusted for multiple comparisons. The benchmark texts predate the models, so contamination cannot be ruled out. Broader Impact Statement Compaction that deletes a question’s evidence can make supported answers “unsupported”. Without provenance, a downstream consumer may take them for answers that are genuinely unsupported or false, and the sufficiency check does not flag every such case. Recoverable full-state designs should be evaluated before compaction is used in consequential settings. Keeping the full state in turn carries the privacy and retention obligations of whatever it contains. Repeat reads. open-decider reads deterministically up to floating point. Each read is one forward pass in evaluation mode with a softmax over option logits, no sampling and a fixed option order.
